ai-852e0910a9.headline: India To Get AI Law, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw Says Centre Will Issue Consultation Paper Soon
ai-852e0910a9.fulltext:
India To Get AI Law, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw Says Centre Will Issue Consultation Paper Soon
Union IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw says proposed consultation paper will seek inputs from citizens, industry and other stakeholders as concerns over AI-generated harms grow.
The Centre is making its move towards a dedicated law to regulate artificial intelligence (AI), as Union Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw announced on Friday that a consultation paper will be issued in the coming weeks.
Speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi on October 23, Vaishnaw said the government would seek views from citizens, industry representatives, experts and other stakeholders before framing its regulatory approach.
“Today the time has come when the risks of AI have crossed a threshold where we should come up with a law and new regulations,” the minister said.
He added that the government was already working on the proposed framework and that the consultation paper would provide an opportunity for different sections of society to share their concerns and suggestions.
“We'll be issuing a consultation paper in the coming weeks. That consultation paper will be where we will seek all the inputs from society, from citizens, from industries, and stakeholders,” Vaishnaw said.
The Union Minister has said businesses were increasingly aware of both the benefits and potential harms associated with AI hence, the government wants to obtain inputs from sectors using the technology to better understand these challenges.
"AI has been adopted very aggressively by our industry. When we talk to the banks, we talk to manufacturing industries, service industries, finance, insurance, and financial services. Everywhere, people are rapidly using AI. There is a good understanding of what good AI can bring, and there is also an understanding of what harm AI can do. That's why that understanding is there today in various sectors. We would like to get input from each of the sectors," he added.
The minister has also stressed the importance of keeping AI systems under human control and ensuring that safeguards are available when systems behave unpredictably.
"The race towards innovation has to be moderated by the safety of human beings. Some principles have already been established. It has to be human first. AI has to be human-centric. It has to make sure that control over the agents, control over the models, control over the outcome that happens, and control over the processes are in human hands. There has to be some equivalent of stopping things if they go out of control. Those principles have already come up," he added.
The consultation paper is expected to help determine the scope and direction of future regulation. The government has emphasised the need for international cooperation, given the cross-border nature of AI technologies and the challenges of regulating systems developed and deployed across jurisdictions.
The consultation process will provide an opportunity to examine how India can address emerging AI-related harms while allowing innovation and wider access to the technology. The eventual framework could have implications for technology companies, digital platforms, businesses using AI and individuals affected by AI-generated content.
India's earlier policy approach had emphasised the use of existing laws and targeted amendments rather than immediately introducing a standalone AI statute. In February the Union Government had notified stringent amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing enhanced obligations on online platforms for the regulation of artificial intelligence-generated and synthetic content, including deepfakes.
Under the amended framework, intermediaries such as social media platforms are required to remove flagged AI-generated or deceptive content within three hours of receiving directions from a court or a competent authority, significantly reducing the earlier compliance window of 36 hours.

global-economics-094ede4a7b.headline: Amazon's cloud is nearly sold out through 2027. Can its AI spending keep up with demand?
global-economics-094ede4a7b.fulltext:
LivemintPublished24 Oct 2026, 09:37 AM IST
Amazon Web Services (AWS) has sold out most of its cloud computing capacity for 2027, with a substantial portion of 2028 capacity already committed, as surging artificial intelligence demand outpaces its infrastructure expansion, chief executive Andy Jassy said.
Speaking on a video podcast with Andreessen Horowitz co-founder Ben Horowitz and general partner Erik Torenberg, Jassy said Amazon was struggling to meet demand from AI laboratories and enterprise customers, despite plans to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditure in 2026.
“2027 is largely sold out. We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference [service] Bedrock, or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks. A good chunk of 2028 is sold out,” Jassy said.
He added that Amazon could justify investing more to meet demand, with much of its 2026 cloud capacity already booked.
The comments highlight the growing pressure on cloud providers to supply the computing power needed to develop and run AI systems. AWS offers cloud infrastructure through services including Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), which provides virtual servers, and Amazon Bedrock, which gives customers access to AI models.
Jassy described AI demand as a “barbell”. AI laboratories are consuming computing resources on an unprecedented scale, while businesses are using AI for specific tasks such as customer service and fraud detection. The middle of the market, where everyday business software has yet to adopt AI widely, remains largely untapped.
He expects this segment could eventually become the largest source of demand as businesses expand their use of AI.
The cost of inference, the computing required when an AI model responds to a prompt or performs a task, remains a barrier to wider adoption.
“It's still an order of magnitude too expensive in my opinion for it to be used as pervasively as possible,” Jassy said, suggesting costs need to fall roughly tenfold for AI to become more widely used.
Amazon is developing its own chips to improve performance and reduce computing costs. Jassy compared the effort with the company's earlier decision to develop Graviton processors when it sought better performance per dollar from server chips.
“We saw that same movie in the AI space,” he said.
Amazon is positioning its Trainium chips as a lower-cost option for AI computing. Jassy said they offer 30% to 40% better price-performance than comparable processors.
“Our chips business is a big piece of that,” he said.
Amazon has disclosed more than $225 billion in future Trainium revenue commitments, including agreements involving Anthropic and OpenAI. Jassy also credited Amazon's investment in Anthropic with supporting its chip efforts.
He described the acquisition of chip design firm Annapurna Labs more than a decade ago as potentially the best deal in Amazon's history. The company helped develop both Trainium and Graviton.
Amazon is scheduled to report its third-quarter results on October 29, when investors will look for further details on cloud growth and infrastructure spending.
(With Reuters Inputs)

indian-startups-d75d959636.headline: Myntra Slips Into The Red In FY26, Reports ₹582 Cr Loss
indian-startups-d75d959636.fulltext: Fashion ecommerce platform Myntra reported a net loss of ₹581.8 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26), reversing a net profit of ₹546.3 Cr in the previous fiscal. Myntra’s operating revenue fell 13.5% to ₹5,242.5 Cr in the fiscal under review, compared to ₹6,063.8 Cr in FY25. Myntra earns revenue from three streams – marketplace services, logistics services and advertisement services. Breaking down the top line, marketplace and collection services contributed to 50.7%. It stood at ₹2,657.3 Cr in FY26, marking a 3% increase from ₹2,580.2 Cr in the previous year. Advertisement Services rose 35.2% to ₹1,236.4 Cr in the year under review, from ₹914.5 Cr in FY25. Meanwhile, logistics and shipping services fell 53.2% to ₹1,119.2 Cr in FY2025-26, from ₹2,390.5 Cr a year ago. Besides these, other operating revenue contributed ₹229.6 Cr, taking the overall topline to ₹5,242.5 Cr in the reported year. Including other income of ₹73.3 Cr, the total income for the fiscal year FY26 stood at ₹5,315.8 Cr, a 13.4% fall from ₹6,137 Cr. The company’s EBITDA loss stood at ₹435 Cr in FY26, from ₹535.9 Cr in FY25. Founded in 2007 by Mukesh Bansal, Ashutosh Lawania and Vineet Saxena, Myntra is an online marketplace which allows third-party sellers to sell their fashion products. The Bengaluru-based startup was acquired by Flipkart for $240 Mn in 2014. Earlier this year, Flipkart Fashion’s Sharon Pais was elevated to the role of the head of fashion marketplace arm Myntra, replacing Nandita Sinha. Additionally, Myntra also appointed Instacart executive Pramod Adiddam as its chief technology officer (CTO). Myntra’s parent, Flipkart Group, also released its consolidated FY26 financials following its reverse flip to India. The Walmart-backed ecommerce group saw an 18.2% jump in consolidated revenue from operations to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr while loss narrowed 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr. “At the PAT level, net loss reduced by approximately ₹180 Cr year over year. The improvement was moderated by higher finance costs, the derecognition of deferred tax assets recognised in earlier periods and certain one-off exceptional items,” the company said in a blog post. Zooming Into Myntra’s FY26 Expenses Total expenses for the year 2025-26 remained nearly flat, with a 0.6% increase to ₹5,757.7 Cr, from ₹5,726 Cr in the previous year. Here is a closer look at where the ecommerce platform spent the most: Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenses towards salaries, wages, bonus, staff welfare, gratuity and provident fund, Myntra spent ₹776.9 Cr in the year under review, up 3.8% from ₹748.8 Cr in FY25. Direct Expenses: Constituting 32% of the total expenses, this includes payment gateway charges and logistic charges. Direct expenses stood at ₹1,841 Cr, marking a 13.9% decline from ₹2,139.4 Cr. Advertisement And Promotion Expenses: Spending under this head rose 10.5% to ₹2,326.5 Cr, compared to ₹2,105.3 Cr, contributing 40.4% of the overall expenditure.

indian-startups-60f5419e6d.headline: IPO-Bound Garuda Aerospace’s FY26 Profit Jumps 41% To ₹25.9 Cr
indian-startups-60f5419e6d.fulltext: Chennai-based dronetech startup Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹25.9 Cr in FY26, growing 41.1% from ₹18.4 Cr from the previous fiscal year. In terms of operational profitability, the drone maker’s EBITA for the fiscal year jumped 31.8% to ₹35.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹26.6 Cr in the FY25. Operating revenue surged 66.8% YoY to ₹206 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹123.5 Cr in the previous year. Sales of drones and drone parts brought in ₹99.4 Cr to the top line while the remaining ₹106.5 Cr via sale of services. Another ₹15 Lakh was earned from delivery charges. Including other income of ₹26.5 Lakh, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹206.2 Cr. “During the year, we continued to strengthen our manufacturing capabilities, expand our Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) operations, deepen our investment in indigenous research and development, and build strategic partnerships in India and international markets. We also advanced our capabilities in artificial intelligence, autonomous flight, data analytics, defence systems and specialised mission platforms,” cofounder and whole-time director Agnishwar Jayaprakash noted in a message to shareholders. The improvement in the financial performance comes as Garuda’s proposed public listing plans take shape. The startup took the pre-filing route to confidentially submit its draft IPO papers with the SEBI earlier in April. The IPO was greenlit by the markets regulator in August. While the startup is yet to file its updated DRHP for public access, its board approved plans to raise up to ₹750 Cr via the fresh issue component of the proposed IPO back in March. As per reports, the OFS component could result in investors offloading shares worth as much as ₹250 Cr. In its annual report for FY26, the startup disclosed that its board of directors had approved a private placement of equity shares worth ₹57.2 Cr back in August. Investors who backed the startup were Umasankar Nistala, Rakesh Pillai, Jitendra Rana, Vimaan Innovators LLP and Aditum Management. The proceeds of the issue would fuel business growth, working capital requirements, and be used for loan repayments. The startup claims to have become India’s largest drone maker, having manufactured and sold over 3000 drones. It also claimed to be the first drone company to partner with three defence PSUs. It has raised a total funding of over $37 Mn to date from investors like Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle, cricketer Mahendra Singh Dhoni, among others. It was last valued at $250 Mn after raising a $11 Mn Series B funding round led by Venture Catalysts. Where Did Garuda Aerospace Spend In FY26? Garuda Aerospace’s total expenses in FY26 rose 73.2% YoY to ₹172.2 Cr from ₹99.4 Cr in FY25. It reported no exceptional items during the fiscal but bore ₹8.2 Cr tax expenses. Here are the main operational expenses of the startup: Cost of Materials Consumed: Representing the largest operational expense, raw material costs surged 61.5% YoY to ₹116.8 Cr from ₹72.3 Cr in FY25. Impairment Losses on Financial Assets: Impairment losses amounted to ₹11.1 Cr in FY26, compared to ₹6.5 Lakh in the year-ago period. Employee Benefit Expenses: Garuda Aerospace’s personnel-related costs decreased 16.7% YoY to ₹8 Cr in FY26 from ₹9.6 Cr in the previous year. Depreciation And Amortisation Expenses: The cost recorded under this line item increased 13.3% YoY to ₹4.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹3.6 Cr in FY25. Other Expenses: Spending on items like professional expenses, travel, maintenance, rent, and other corporate overheads stayed nearly flat at ₹29.2 Cr.

ai-110fd09f65.headline: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
ai-110fd09f65.fulltext:
Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.
Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew, and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral.
The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.
There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.
“ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.”
SpaceXAI did not respond in time to comment.
Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions.
“It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics.
“If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said.
Previous research has raised similar concerns.
The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing.
The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt.
Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%.
GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.)
The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy.
ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans.
The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote.
Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72.
“If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said.
One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights.
Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat.
When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.”
The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine.
Musk has donated upwards of $445 million in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly quarter of a billion dollars he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year, he said, he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections.
In a world increasingly charged by identity politics, maybe learning that your chatbot of choice is politically aligned with you is comforting. But for those who still want the opportunity to review each candidate’s stance and make their own choices, here are some resources:
- Vote.gov
- League of Women Voters’ vote411.org
- Ballotpedia
- VoteSmart
- FEC.gov and OpenSecrets
- State and county election offices
- Candidates’ websites and local news

deep-tech-c107a673cb.headline: ISRO will not be privatised, says chairperson Narayanan
deep-tech-c107a673cb.fulltext:
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is under the Government of India, and it will not be privatised, the chairperson of the agency, V. Narayanan, said on Saturday (October 24, 2026). However, some of its operations will be performed by the private sector on a commercial basis, he noted.
The remarks come amid questions on whether the Union government intends to transfer the agency’s launch-vehicle and satellite manufacturing to private firms.
“Our space programme is 64 years old, we have as many as 56 satellites. But the demand is for thousands of satellites,” Mr. Narayanan said during a graduation event at Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research, Porur.
Highlighting the Indian Space Policy, 2023, he said that the ISRO will handhold startups and private companies to work in the space sector. “The space ecosystem in the country and the country’s economy will grow, resulting in job opportunities. When a Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) or Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) rocket takes off, 75% of our budget is pumped into the private industries. The private companies are also contributing. People must not misinterpret that as ISRO will be privatised,” the chairperson stressed.
He also noted that the upcoming launch of the navigation satellite, NVS-03, planned for October 30, is going as per schedule and that the launch vehicle was moved to the launch pad on Saturday (October 24).
Talking about the Gaganyaan mission, he said that the rocket is ready and the crew escape system on the rocket module has also been developed. “The environmental and safety system in space has been developed. We plan to send three rockets unmanned and we are working on the first rocket. We will soon test the first rocket and then send the other two unmanned rockets. If all these are successful, then we will send a manned rocket. So far 8,000 experiments have been conducted on land.”
He said that Chandrayaan-4, which will land on the moon and return with a sample, is being planned for 2028.
Certificates distributed
A total of 455 students received their graduation certificates at the convocation ceremony. As many as 217 candidates from postgraduate degrees and 238 from undergraduate courses got their certificates.

world-67efb573cd.headline: Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
world-67efb573cd.fulltext:
Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a social media post.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.
Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.
Reuters contributed reporting

india-38175ab302.headline: Anthropic PB admits to having an Indian subsidiary, contradicts earlier stand in court
india-38175ab302.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-38175ab302.fulltext:
A legal dispute over the use of the name ‘Anthropic’ has taken a new turn after US-based artificial intelligence company Anthropic PBC acknowledged in the Belagavi Commercial Court that a wholly owned subsidiary operates in India.
Belagavi-based Anthropic Softwares Private Limited has claimed to have registered the name of the company and brand much before the US-based firm, and has challenged the use of the company’s name by the American entity.
“In a written statement filed in the court, the company stated that Irina Ghose is the managing director of the India entity. This development raises questions about corporate conduct and the positions taken during the proceedings,” said Mohammad Ayyaz Mulla, Managing Director of Belagavi-based Anthropic Softwares Private Limited.
“For over 10 months, Anthropic India Private Limited resisted being impleaded in the case, maintaining that it was a separate legal entity and disputing the existence of a cause of action against it. More significantly, in an objection supported by an affidavit on oath, its Managing Director, Irina Ghose, denied that Anthropic India was directly or indirectly promoting Anthropic PBC’s business, calling the allegation baseless and requiring strict proof.
“Anthropic PBC’s subsequent written statement refers to its wholly owned Indian subsidiary and identifies Ms. Ghose as its managing director. We want to ask whether these positions, considered together, reflected the transparency and professional ethics expected of a global technology company. He said the court should examine whether procedural objections were being used to delay consideration of the core dispute over prior use of the ‘Anthropic’ name.”
Mr. Mulla alleged that repeated misdirected emails intended for Anthropic PBC had reached his company despite regular notifications, creating business disruption, brand confusion, and potential data-security risk, including the possibility of sensitive communications reaching unintended recipients. He said the continuing problem raised serious questions about whether customer confidentiality and corrective action were receiving adequate attention. He urged the US company to demonstrate its belief in corporate ethics through its behaviour.
Published - October 22, 2026 09:46 am IST

ai-2bca17fd43.headline: Three fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were never told what they actually leaked
ai-2bca17fd43.fulltext:
Three fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were never told what they actually leaked
Key Points
- Three OpenAI safety researchers who were fired deny sharing confidential information.
- They suspect their terminations were tied to their efforts to make AI models easier to monitor and warn that the case could discourage employees from raising safety concerns.
- OpenAI cited alleged policy violations. The researchers say investigators focused on their Signal chats with outside researchers, though OpenAI said Signal was not the reason for the firings.
The three OpenAI safety researchers who were fired over alleged leaks are telling their side of the story. Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang deny sharing confidential information, question the official reasoning behind their termination, and suspect a connection to their advocacy for more transparent AI systems.
OpenAI dismissed all three after an internal investigation into alleged violations of its policies on handling sensitive information. Each of them had spoken publicly about AI risks before being let go.
In interviews with the Wall Street Journal, the researchers now dispute that account. OpenAI told the Journal that the firings had nothing to do with safety concerns the researchers had raised. But the three say they were never told in writing which information they supposedly mishandled. They also worry the case could discourage independent safety auditors from working with AI companies altogether.
The Journal's reporting sheds light on what led to the confrontation. OpenAI's security team suspected the three of sharing details about the company's internal model architecture with an external safety researcher and asked them to unlock their personal phones. On those devices, the team found Signal chats with disappearing messages enabled. A week later, all three were fired at the same time. OpenAI said Signal was not an approved communication tool but insisted it was not the reason for the terminations. Korbak counters that disappearing messages are a routine security practice across Silicon Valley.
A dispute over monitoring AI reasoning steps
The dispute centers on a technical question with major consequences. Should AI companies let outsiders inspect how their models think? Reasoning models can record the intermediate steps of their problem-solving process on an internal scratchpad known as the chain of thought. Companies and safety researchers rely on these traces to understand how models arrive at their decisions.
In a 2025 paper, Balesni, Korbak, and Wang joined leading researchers from several AI labs in calling for continued access to this capability. The issue grew more urgent over the summer, when employees at AI companies began discussing models that think longer but write down fewer intermediate steps. Balesni pushed back internally by sharing a related proposal from Ryan Greenblatt, then chief scientist at Redwood Research.
Korbak, too, was in regular contact with Greenblatt. The two communicated over Slack and Signal while working together on the analysis of a high-profile incident—the attack by OpenAI agents on Hugging Face—for which Greenblatt had been hired by METR to conduct an independent investigation.
A news report about Astra kicked off the investigation
That cooperation became a liability after The Information reported on September 1 that OpenAI's new model Astra was more capable but revealed less of its reasoning process. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki dismissed the report as muddled at the time on X, even though he himself had warned of an industry-wide race toward models that can no longer be monitored.
A few weeks later, OpenAI launched an internal leak investigation, according to the Journal. Balesni says investigators named Greenblatt as the suspected source and demanded to see the Signal chats with him. Greenblatt denies passing confidential information to journalists.
Wang faced a separate accusation: OpenAI said she had repeatedly accessed an executive's inbox. She says she had asked nearly a year earlier for that access to be revoked, accidentally opened a sensitive email the previous month, did not share its contents, and reported the incident right away. OpenAI says the access itself was not the issue.
The fallout extends well beyond the three of them, according to Korbak. Colleagues are now afraid to talk to outsiders or raise safety concerns internally, he says. In a letter to OpenAI's board, the three researchers call for closer cooperation with external safety organizations.
Separately, a recently published on-site audit raised its own questions about OpenAI's safety practices. Staff from METR and Redwood Research found numerous security gaps in OpenAI's infrastructure during the review, but OpenAI redacted nearly half the final report.
OpenAI also published its own report on a new security architecture that operates without internet access and said it fixed the issues and resumed training in early October. The company says it will announce several new external partnerships soon.

ai-568daa5fc7.headline: AI funding fears rattle Wall Street. Here's how we're adjusting our portfolio
ai-568daa5fc7.fulltext: Wall Street struggled to find its footing last week as renewed concerns about financing the artificial intelligence boom overshadowed strong earnings. An early rebound in AI-related names ran into a brick wall Thursday after Meta Platforms reported negative free cash flow for the first time since its 2012 initial public offering. The sell-off spread to more defensive areas of the market Friday, sending the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% as oil prices surged on fears of renewed U.S. strikes against Iran. The Nasdaq only posted a slight loss as investors returned to beaten-down chip stocks and bought up cyber stocks. The S & P 500 on Friday was modestly lower. For the week, the Dow was the big winner, rising 0.4%. The S & P 500 was down 0.5%, while the Nasdaq slipped 0.7%. Here's a closer look at the three developments that drove last week's market action. AI funding fears deepen The AI trade remained volatile last week as investors weighed strong demand against growing concerns about how companies will finance the massive infrastructure buildout. AI stocks rallied early in the week, especially on SpaceX 's surging revenue numbers reported Tuesday evening . Thursday was terrible. In addition to cash flow concerns, Meta's strong earnings from Wednesday evening were overshadowed by its disclosure that its long-term plans could require hundreds of billions of dollars in additional financing. CoreWeave , which has become a focal point for concerns about debt-fueled AI spending, fell 10% Thursday as investors continued to scrutinize its borrowing costs. It was down more than 10% for the week after the neocloud ended the prior week down more than 25%. Even Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged the funding challenge, saying Thursday that the "demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital." The issue isn't AI demand, but whether companies can secure enough financing to meet it as borrowing becomes more expensive. Nvidia was down roughly 1.5% last week. We took advantage of Thursday's sell-off to buy 10 shares of GE Vernova , our first AI-related purchase in five weeks, and upgraded the stock to our buy-equivalent 1 rating on confidence in long-term power demand. But we also reduced our exposure to the broader AI trade. "The collapse of the data center requires us to circle the wagons," Jim Cramer said. "We can't have too much of the ones we have. We can pick as we did with GEV, but nothing aggressive. And all tag ends should go like Broadcom." He continued: "Circling means we want to be bigger in the better ones." To that end, we exited Broadcom on Friday, locking in an average gain of roughly 128%. We also trimmed CrowdStrike , realizing a gain of about 187%, to right-size the position rather than because of concerns about its fundamentals. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks were our two biggest winners last week — both up more than 11% as news of the security flaws in the PHP programming language touched off a global security scramble. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz told CNBC Friday that AI-powered attacks observed by CrowdStrike doubled each month from July through September. Jim has said all along that cyber is needed more than ever in the new world of AI. Unpacking Meta's wild week Meta delivered a strong third quarter Wednesday evening, but worries about negative free cash flow and its AI spending needs upstaged strong guidance and a promising roadmap for its viral Muse AI agent. What made Thursday's 7% drop in Meta shares even more painful was that it had been rallying in after-hours trading on Wednesday night on encouraging signs for Muse. While a muted capital expenditure outlook was initially viewed as a positive on earnings night, a regulatory filing from Meta quickly raised fresh concerns about its funding needs. The company warned that its long-term plans could require raising "hundreds of billions of dollars over a period of several years beginning as early as fall 2026." The filing shed more light on Meta's plan to create a new class of non-voting stock, Class C, in January to help finance investments and acquisitions without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's voting control. The new share class would basically facilitate a two-for-one stock split, with holders getting one Class C share for every Class A they own. While encouraged by early Muse traction and Meta's strong core digital advertising business, we want greater clarity on how those investments will be funded and monetized. We maintained our hold-equivalent 2 rating on Meta stock and $800 price target. Meta stock lost more than 9% on the week. Bright spots in the portfolio The rotation out of AI stocks benefited several defensive portfolio holdings last week, reinforcing the importance of diversification . Kimberly-Clark jumped 4.3% as investors sought safety in consumer staples. Home Depot increased 3.3%, benefiting from the 10-year Treasury yield going below 5%, which could help revive housing activity and home improvement spending. Johnson & Johnson surged 3.2%, recovering all its post-earnings losses as investors rotated into healthcare. There were also encouraging developments for Apple and Qnity Electronics . Apple's new foldable iPhone Duo is off to a strong start, with delivery wait times exceeding three months. While supply constraints are contributing to the delays, strong demand suggests the device could become another growth engine. The Duo became available in stores for walk-in customers on Friday. Apple shares rose about 1.2% for the week. The iPhone maker also expanded its partnership with Qnity , which will produce advanced films for the 18 Pro's new camera system. The deeper relationship is encouraging, though our investment thesis remains centered on Qnity's fast-growing data center business. Qnity shares fell more than 4.5% for the week on the recent data center trade troubles, though far less than GE Vernova's over 11% weekly drop. Watch out video tour of Qnity labs outside Boston. indian-startups-5c11a27448.headline: Zetwerk shares list at over 5% premium in stock market debut
indian-startups-5c11a27448.fulltext:
Bengaluru-based Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses made a positive debut on the stock exchanges on Friday, with its shares listing at a 5.5% premium over the IPO price.
According to exchange data, the company shares opened at Rs 159.25 on the National Stock Exchange (NSE), compared with the issue price of Rs 151 per share.
On the final day of the IPO, the qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) portion received the highest demand, with 4.73X subscription, followed by the non-institutional investors (NIIs) category at 1.4X. The employee quota was subscribed 1.58X, while the retail portion saw weaker demand at 0.72X.
Ahead of the IPO, Zetwerk raised Rs 2,251 crore from anchor investors, including global investors such as Capital Group, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and Nomura, alongside domestic investors such as SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund and HDFC Mutual Fund.
According to its RHP, the issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 2,830 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 14.45 crore shares worth Rs 2,182 crore by existing shareholders.
The company plans to use a portion of the fresh issue proceeds to repay debt, with the remaining funds earmarked for acquisitions, strategic investments and general corporate purposes.
On the financial front, Zetwerk’s revenue from continuing operations grew 40.4% to Rs 15,913 crore in FY26 from Rs 11,332 crore in FY25. In Q1 FY27, revenue from operations rose 55% year-on-year to Rs 4,118 crore, while losses from continuing operations narrowed 93% to Rs 64 crore from Rs 881 crore in the year-ago period.

indian-startups-950a336353.headline: Flipkart-Backed super.money’s FY26 Revenue Triples To ₹292 Cr
indian-startups-950a336353.fulltext: UPI provider super.money reported a net loss of ₹263.8 Cr in FY26, 78.5% higher than ₹147.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue more than tripled to ₹292.4 Cr from ₹88.8 Cr in FY25. Its loan marketplace contributed around 84.7% of its revenue. Combined with other income of ₹90 Lakh, its total income amounted to ₹293.3 Cr. super.money did not report any tax expenses or exceptional items, resulting in a total comprehensive loss of ₹262.9 Cr. super.money was launched by the Walmart-owned Flipkart in 2024 and is led by founder and CEO Prakash Sikaria, who was the senior vice president at Flipkart, helming its ads business, Shopsy, Cleartrip and Yantra. super.money’s core business is enabling UPI payments and is the fifth largest player in the market. In September 2026, it processed over 40.51 Cr UPI transactions, collectively worth more than ₹19,613.3 Cr. Besides, the startup has now also ventured into loan facilitation, connecting borrowers with banks and NBFCs. It also enables users to book fixed deposits and partners with banks to offer co-branded credit cards. Where Did super.money Spend? super.money’s total expenses in FY26 surged 130% YoY to ₹557.1 Cr from ₹241.8 Cr in the previous fiscal. Let’s dive into a breakdown of its spending. Business Promotion Expenses: This was the biggest expenditure, rising 3.34X YoY to ₹341 Cr in FY26. Employee Benefits Expense: Employee costs grew 73.8% YoY to ₹138.1 Cr compared to ₹79.5 Cr in the year-ago period. Marketplace Charges: Spending on this line item fell 64.2% YoY to ₹15.6 Cr from ₹43.5 Cr. Finance Costs: super.money’s finance-related expenses skyrocketed to ₹11.1 Cr in the year under review from ₹0.1 Cr in the previous year. Other Expenses: Other operating expenses including outside contracted services and communication charges increased 177.2% YoY to ₹47.9 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹17.3 Cr in FY25.

deep-tech-673a4a769b.headline: China’s AI compute surge heavily reliant on US chips, offshore cloud access: report
deep-tech-673a4a769b.fulltext:
Search the way you think. Try our AI-powered search to find news faster.
China’s access to artificial intelligence computing power will double next year, but US-designed chips will account for about 65 per cent of that capacity, an indication of its continued reliance on foreign hardware, according to new research.
Total compute available to Chinese entities was expected to expand in 2027 from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million “H100-equivalents” – a metric benchmarked against Nvidia’s data-centre graphics processing units, according to a report by the Washington-based Institute for Progress (IFP).
To project these figures, IFP said it tallied domestic chips, legal imports, smuggled processors and compute accessed remotely via overseas cloud networks. Remote access alone was expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year, according to the report published this week.
While the US maintains a roughly 16-fold advantage in AI training compute over China, leading Chinese models lag their American rivals by only 6.5 months, the report said.
IFP pointed to distillation – where developers train systems on the outputs of superior AI models – as a key factor helping China close the gap. China has previously rejected US allegations of “aggressive, malicious” AI distillation by domestic developers as groundless.
In light of the findings, the institute urged US policymakers to impose stricter controls on overseas cloud access, chip smuggling and legal exports.
A separate report published on Tuesday by the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy stated that US-designed compute power remained legally available for rent to foreign entities otherwise barred from buying the hardware.
The Washington-based policy group called on the US Bureau of Industry and Security to restrict Chinese access to cloud capacity large enough for training frontier AI models or running them at scale, while advocating for stronger checks on customer identity and ownership.
While chip exports are subject to licensing restrictions, Washington moved in January to allow case-by-case export reviews for Nvidia’s H200, Advanced Micro Devices’ MI325X and comparable processors under security conditions.
American exporters must show that sales would not divert supply from US customers, while Chinese buyers must adopt formal export compliance procedures and submit chips for independent testing within the US.
Meanwhile, Chinese tech giants are scrambling to bolster domestic alternatives. Huawei Technologies last month said its Ascend 960DT chip, designed for AI model training, would become available in the first quarter of 2027 – three quarters ahead of its original schedule.
The Shenzhen-based firm revealed that more than 1,000 of its Atlas 900 A3 SuperPoDs had already been deployed, while its Atlas 950 system had entered large-scale commercial use. These cluster architectures link thousands of individual processors to handle demanding AI workloads.
In an updated report last month, San Francisco-based research group Epoch AI identified high-bandwidth memory – a crucial component for feeding data to AI chips – as the main constraint on Huawei’s output.
Epoch AI estimated that Huawei’s chip output this year would deliver less than 4 per cent of the computing power of Nvidia’s global shipments.
Howard Liu is a Beijing-based technology and business reporter at the South China Morning Post, covering the semiconductor industry, AI and global tech supply chains. Previously at Caixin Media, he focused on China’s AI, semiconductor and cloud computing sectors. A graduate of Columbia University, he enjoys running, swimming and hiking.

deep-tech-98747dad4a.headline: German drone maker Quantum Systems claims 483-mph speed for battery-powered experimental aircraft
deep-tech-98747dad4a.fulltext:
LivemintPublished24 Oct 2026, 08:23 PM IST
German drone manufacturer Quantum Systems has announced that its battery-powered experimental aircraft, Apex Recordhunter, reached a speed of 483 mph (777 km/h) during a record attempt, potentially setting a new benchmark for battery-electric flight.
However, the achievement has not yet been officially confirmed, as the aircraft must complete a return flight to account for the effects of wind, reported Interesting Engineering.
The latest test highlights advances in electric propulsion technology and provides engineers with an opportunity to assess the performance and limitations of battery-powered aircraft operating at extremely high speeds.
Quantum Systems said the findings from the experiment would contribute to its ongoing drone development programmes, including technologies designed to counter fast-moving aerial threats.
The latest reported speed exceeds the 434 mph (699 km/h) achieved by the Apex Recordhunter during a test in June. At the time, the company described the performance as an unofficial world-best for a battery-electric flying object.
Developed by Quantum Systems' experimental N3XT team in Germany over approximately a year, the Apex Recordhunter is a technology demonstrator rather than an operational aircraft.
The project allows engineers to evaluate electric propulsion, energy management and high-speed flight performance. The latest run pushed the aircraft's reported speed to more than 200 metres per second, demonstrating the power requirements associated with rapid battery-electric flight.
Despite the reported achievement, the company has not disclosed detailed specifications for the aircraft's battery capacity, motor, energy consumption or flight duration.
Quantum Systems said the aircraft uses specialised battery cells developed by a Porsche subsidiary. However, detailed technical information about the battery pack and propulsion system has not been released.
Achieving high speeds with battery-powered aircraft requires careful management of energy consumption and propulsion performance.
The aircraft must generate sufficient power to maintain its speed while preserving stability and operating within the limitations of its electrical systems.
The Apex project is intended to help engineers understand these challenges and identify improvements that could be applied to future aircraft designs.
The reported 483-mph run is not yet an officially established record. A return leg is required to account for wind effects and validate the aircraft's performance under the applicable record-attempt procedure.
Quantum Systems said the experience gained through the project would inform its future development efforts.
Beyond experimental flight, Quantum Systems said technologies developed through the Apex programme could support its work on interceptor drones designed to counter increasingly fast aerial threats.
The company has pointed to Russia's jet-powered Geran drones, which can reportedly reach speeds of 311 to 373 mph (500 to 600 km/h).
The increasing speed of such aircraft creates challenges for interception systems, potentially requiring faster and more capable drones to respond effectively.
Quantum Systems said its work on electric propulsion, energy management and high-speed flight was helping inform the development of interceptor technologies.
However, the company has clarified that the Apex Recordhunter itself is not a weapon and does not share hardware with its combat systems.
The Apex Recordhunter programme illustrates how experimental aircraft can help manufacturers evaluate emerging propulsion technologies before applying the findings to other systems.
Although the reported speed remains subject to official confirmation, the test provides additional data on the potential capabilities of battery-electric aircraft.
Quantum Systems has not yet announced when the record attempt will be formally validated. The results of further testing will help determine how the technology could contribute to future high-speed drone development.

deep-tech-54cac0b515.headline: Arm Comments on Jury Decision in Qualcomm Trial
deep-tech-54cac0b515.fulltext:
Arm’s Ami Badani cites the $2 nominal damages award as validation, while chip design experts point to open architectures such as RISC-V as the long-term alternative for AI workload flexibility.
Following our initial coverage of the Delaware federal jury verdict in the Qualcomm and Arm dispute, Arm contacted EE Times to clarify the IP vendor’s position. In a phone interview with EE Times, Arm CMO Ami Badani discussed the company’s stance on the jury’s decision and the stakes surrounding licensing negotiations for Arm’s next-generation v10 architecture.
Badani contended that Arm emerged as a “victor” in court due to the nominal $2 damages award and the presiding judge’s reluctance to oversee future licensing terms, while emphasizing the ongoing technical and commercial collaboration with Qualcomm.
She also commented on the rise of other architectures such as RISC-V, as experts caution that restrictive proprietary frameworks may compel semiconductor designers toward open standards to meet the demands of evolving AI workloads.
Badani, who attended several proceedings in Wilmington, argued that the jury’s decision to award Qualcomm just $2 in nominal damages supports Arm’s position. The jury awarded $1 for a licensing breach and $1 for interference with Qualcomm’s business relationship with Meta, while finding for Arm on other allegations.
She argued that the minimal financial penalty supported Arm’s position that it operated in good faith throughout its licensing relationship with Qualcomm and that its conduct did not warrant substantial monetary damages.
Badani cited recent Bloomberg reporting on closing arguments in the case before U.S. District Judge Maryellen Noreika. During the hearing, Judge Noreika expressed strong reservations about Qualcomm’s request for the court to compel Arm to negotiate in good faith new licensing terms for its upcoming v10 architecture.
The judge characterized Qualcomm’s bid for judicial oversight of commercial terms as “very, very drastic,” remarking that the court would not step in to regulate Arm’s business practices or act as a regulatory supervisor.
Furthermore, Badani cited the court’s reluctance to dictate contractual rates or grant additional financial remedies as further support for Arm’s position. She also indicated that a final written ruling on the remaining antitrust and licensing claims could take several weeks, as both corporate parties complete their final written submissions for judicial review.
Despite the four-year court battle, Badani emphasized that Arm and Qualcomm maintain ongoing technical and commercial collaboration. She noted that, in Arm’s view, Qualcomm is not actively seeking further monetary compensation, but rather attempting to maximize the commercial and technical value derived from its ongoing licensing relationship.
Badani also directly addressed industry analysis suggesting that open-standard instruction set architectures, specifically RISC-V, are the primary beneficiaries of the legal conflict between two of the semiconductor sector’s largest partners. She rejected claims that RISC-V is capturing significant commercial market share from proprietary architectures in mainstream global markets.
According to Badani, RISC-V is not obtaining meaningful traction as an alternative processor architecture outside of China. She attributed its growth in China’s domestic market primarily to substantial state financial backing and direct government push, rather than organic commercial displacement of established instruction sets in international markets.
Her comments contrast with views from Qualcomm and prominent computer architecture researchers evaluating long-term hardware trends. Last week, Akeana, a U.S. semiconductor startup that designs processors using RISC-V architecture, was acquired by Qualcomm. Akeana’s CEO confirmed the acquisition in a LinkedIn post.
As AI algorithms and models advance rapidly, chip designers need flexibility to modify processor cores, add specialized microarchitectural features, and improve overall energy efficiency.
“As AI is evolving, chip designers need total flexibility to adapt their cores with new functions and improve performance,” Mateo Valero, director of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), told EE Times. “Relying on closed ISAs such as Arm limits the freedom and the possibility to implement new capabilities and improve power consumption. Even the largest companies using Arm’s IP with full architectural licenses have difficulties optimizing their designs due to Arm’s tight conditions and limited support. That’s why we believe that open standard ISAs such as RISC-V offer the best alternative.”
Ultimately, Arm views the $2 nominal damages award and the court’s reluctance to intervene in licensing negotiations as validation of its good-faith practices. However, the implications of the four-year legal battle extend far beyond the Wilmington courtroom. Although Arm and Qualcomm continue to collaborate on technical matters and product roadmaps, the legal friction highlights a pivotal juncture for chip designers.

global-economics-48d475ec4a.headline: Google DeepMind Pentagon AI contract resignations: Researchers exit over classified military deals; all you need to know
global-economics-48d475ec4a.fulltext:
Aachal ManiyarPublished24 Oct 2026, 11:47 PM IST Several Google DeepMind staff have resigned in recent weeks over the company’s AI agreements with the US military. The exits centre on contracts that let the Pentagon use Google’s models in classified settings, where the company has limited visibility and no clear veto power over final uses. Researchers who have left say the deals, signed earlier this year, expand the scope of government applications beyond what they expected when they joined. They worry that existing safeguards and human oversight may not be enough once systems move onto air-gapped military networks. London-based research engineer Sofia Liguori left this week after three years at DeepMind. She told The Intercept she could no longer stay at a company building technology that “automatically makes it easier to escalate the brutality of war.” In an internal letter she wrote that she no longer believes the technology will have a net positive impact on society and urged remaining colleagues to “stay human.” AI researcher Andreas Kirsch resigned earlier in October. He told the BBC that Google’s governance and oversight are “not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings.” Kirsch has also said current models are “not robust enough” for such use and that Google appears to have little ability to monitor how its systems are applied after delivery. Both pointed to the same core issue: once models enter classified environments under “any lawful government purpose” language, the company loses practical control. Notably, staff have raised similar worries about Google’s work with Israeli military systems through Project Nimbus. According to the company, employees have dedicated channels to raise ethical concerns and that policies prohibit retaliation. Google has previously said its agreements include conditions on mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. Departing staff have described those limits as weaker in practice than the company claims. Internal resistance is not new. In April, roughly 600 employees signed a petition asking leadership to avoid classified military work. Research scientist Alex Turner, who worked on AI safety at DeepMind for more than two years, resigned in June. In a July blog post, he wrote that senior management had insisted Google would not sign, yet the deal went ahead. “At that point, I couldn’t stay at Google in good conscience, so I left,” Turner said. The resignations arrive as the Pentagon pushes to integrate advanced AI across classified networks. For Google, the contracts are part of broader government business. global-economics-2f8b56707f.headline: Big action! Who is Avadhut Sathe? Why SEBI ordered Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy to refund ₹546 cr - What he did?
global-economics-2f8b56707f.fulltext:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) took action against Indian stock markets and options trader, Avadhut Sathe, and his trading academy, for running an unregistered investment advisory and research analyst business.
The markets regulator, on Friday, directed Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy Private Limited (ASTAPL) and its founder to refund  ₹546.17 crore collected from participants for providing unregistered investment advisory and research analyst services, along with interest of  ₹67.87 crore.
Who is Avadhut Sathe?
Avadhut Sathe started trading and investment in 1991. As per his trading academy’s official website, Sathe regularly conducts seminars in stock market trading since February 2008.
His academy branches are located in multiple cities including Mumbai, Delhi, Navi Mumbai, Pune Hyderabad, Indore, Nashik, etc. The ASTAPL academy runs multiple programmes linked to stock market investment and trading, including eye opener sessions, Geo Program, SMM, PAPA, etc.
Why did SEBI order a refund by Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy?
SEBI has imposed a total penalty of  ₹11.5 crore on the academy, Sathe and Gouri Avadhut Sathe for violations of securities market regulations. As per SEBI’s 171-page final order, Sathe has been fined  ₹4 crore, while Gouri Avadhut Sathe has been penalised  ₹1.5 crore.
SEBI has barred the academy and Avadhut Sathe from accessing the securities market for two years, or until they fulfil the direction to initiate all refunds.
The regulator found that the academy and Sathe provided investment advice and research recommendations through paid programmes, sessions and WhatsApp groups without obtaining the required registration.
It also found that misleading promotional representations about returns were used to attract participants and that investment advice was provided without assessing the suitability of recommendations for recipients.
Sathe had collected around  ₹601.38 crore from course
The SEBI order stated that the academy and Sathe had collected around  ₹601.38 crore from course participants since inception. However, based on the evidence examined, fees of  ₹546.17 crore attributable to the relevant programmes were identified for disgorgement and refund. 
Now, the markets regulator has directed the academy and Sathe to complete the refund in five months of receiving the order. SEBI has also directed Sathe to publish notices in newspapers within 30 days, explaining the procedure for investors to claim refunds.

climate-energy-26a7d4e7e1.headline: Plugging storage into India’s rooftop solar revolution
climate-energy-26a7d4e7e1.fulltext:
Rooftop solar is now growing rapidly in India, and in the process, it is lowering daytime demand and increasing daytime solar exports. Adding battery storage alongside rooftop solar can turn these phenomena into a source of distributed flexibility.
India’s rooftop solar capacity is growing rapidly, driven by rising domestic adoption under the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana. This short analysis examines how this growth is reshaping demand and grid exports from rooftop solar systems, the challenges posed by existing metering and settlement arrangements, and how storage-linked incentives and evolving settlement mechanisms can help build flexibility within rooftop solar capacity.
A battery subsidy delivered through the existing PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana scheme can turn India’s residential rooftop solar boom into a distributed flexibility resource for the grid. By offering a subsidy on battery capital expenditure to even half of current scheme’s target for approximately INR 280 billion in the next tranche, India could build 15-25 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of storage capacity across households, in what could be a win-win for both consumers and the electricity grid.
Rooftop solar is growing rapidly in India, with households increasingly driving this expansion. Its impact on the grid depends in part on who installs it. Commercial and industrial (C&I) consumers typically size rooftop solar systems to align with their electricity demand, allowing them to consume most of their solar generation on-site. Households, by contrast, tend to consume less electricity during the day and more in the evening. As a result, they export a larger share of their solar generation to the grid during the day and draw electricity back after sunset.
These behind-the-meter exports are decentralised and difficult to forecast or control yet can aggregate into significant volumes at the system level. Battery storage alongside rooftop solar offers a way to manage these exports by shifting surplus generation from solar hours to periods of higher demand. However, the current net metering framework with unrestricted banking and time-blind withdrawal of solar generation reduces the financial incentive for households to add storage. The mechanism treats a unit exported during solar hours as equal to a unit drawn in the evening, though representative market prices can differ six-fold between the two. Net metering regime also affects electricity distribution companies (DISCOMs) as households are billed only on their net consumption, the units removed from their bills are the most expensive ones at the top of the tariff slabs, so DISCOM revenue falls by more than an estimate based on the average tariff would suggest. Overall, even though the system-level value of reducing daytime exports can be significant, the current net metering mechanism does not facilitate the same. This creates a case for incentivising the batteries.
As rooftop solar penetration grows, metering and settlement mechanisms will also need to evolve. Plugging batteries unlock a phased policy evolution, which better aligns consumer economics with system needs and will create a more sustainable path for India’s rooftop solar boom.
India’s rooftop solar boom is an opportunity to get ahead of the grid challenge, rather than wait for it to arrive. With more than 5 million households already adopting rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar, we should be building storage alongside that capacity, not years later. The experience of markets like Australia and the US shows that as rooftop solar scales, its value increasingly depends on when its electricity is used, not just how much it generates. India can learn that lesson early, making batteries a win for consumers and the grid.
Rooftop solar accounts for 19% of India’s total installed solar capacity as of July 2026, concentrated in ten Indian states.
India’s total installed solar capacity reached 164.6 GW in July 2026, of which 30.7 GW comes from rooftop solar capacity, i.e., one in every 5 GW of solar capacity is on rooftops. This rooftop solar share tripled since 2019 from 6% to 19%, demonstrating a significant growth led by Gujarat, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.
Residential rooftop solar capacity under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana stood at 14.9 GW across 5 million households as of July 2026, with ~88% of it concentrated in ten states.
Adding a 5-kWh battery to a 3-kW rooftop system can drastically cut daytime solar exports. However, under the current metering mechanism, it stretches the household’s payback period from around 3.3 years for solar alone to over 9 years, building a case for financial incentive to the households. For example, a 50% subsidy for battery storage under the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana can cut the payback period down to under 7 years.
Over the past decade, utility-scale projects drove India’s solar power growth. As recently as the fiscal year (FY) 2019, rooftop solar accounted for only around 6% of installed solar capacity despite its high potential. But since 2024, after the launch of the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, rooftop solar has surged especially in the residential consumer category. By July 2026, rooftop solar capacity grew three-fold to 30.7 GW, taking its share in India’s total solar capacity of 165 GW to nearly 19%. The share makes it increasingly relevant to the operation and planning of the power system.
Policies had been trying to encourage rooftop solar adoption for some time. In 2014, the roll-out of the Grid Connected Rooftop and Small Solar Power Plants Programme (RTS programme) and the National Solar Mission’s set target of 40 GW by 2022 are examples of the policy push. However, for many years, capacity addition remained subdued, constrained by a lack of consumer awareness, high upfront costs and limited access to affordable financing. Rooftop solar was also not sufficiently cost-effective, particularly for residential consumers, to be an attractive investment without targeted subsidies.
For commercial & industrial (C&I) consumers, however, rooftop solar has been a low-hanging fruit, especially for C&I consumers with access to finance, available rooftop space, and a commitment to decarbonisation.
Installation in the residential category only picked up significantly and widely after the announcement of PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana in 2024. The scheme aims to install 10 million rooftop solar systems and provides residential consumers a capital subsidy of INR 30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW, and INR 18,000 per kW for additional capacity up to 3 kW, subject to a ceiling of INR 78,000 per system. The amendment to the Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules also exempted systems up to 10 kW from technical feasibility studies, placed the cost of any distribution system strengthening for systems up to 5 kW on the distribution company. It also halved the commissioning timeline to fifteen days.
India’s 30.7 GW of rooftop solar capacity as of July 2026 is highly concentrated, with more than 85% installed across just ten states. Gujarat and Maharashtra alone account for close to 45% of the national total, with installed capacity of 7,518 MW and 5,975.8 MW, respectively. The next tier of states, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh, each host between 900 MW and 2,400 MW, while the remaining states and union territories together add up to just over 4,291 MW.
This concentration persists largely because of a variation in retail supply tariffs across states, state-level rooftop solar policies, and overall ecosystem and prosumers’ spending capacity. States use a mix of interventions such as capital subsidies, generation-based incentives and building mandates to drive rooftop solar adoption.
As a result of uneven expansion of rooftop solar across states, system planners now need to factor in a new element to keep the electricity grid stable. The rate of rooftop solar capacity addition and scale of rooftop solar capacity relative to a state’s own peak demand, which may or may not coincide with solar hours, needs monitoring.
As of July 2026, Kerala, Gujarat and Maharashtra had rooftop solar capacity equivalent to 35%, 26% and 18% of their respective peak demand recorded between April and July 2026, compared with 11% nationally. As this share rises, the gap between daytime solar generation and evening demand can widen, increasing the need for grid flexibility and making these states more likely to face balancing challenges ahead of others.
Narrowing the lens to the residential segment under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana shows that rooftop solar capacity stood at 14.9 GW as of July 2026, covering 5 million households and accounting for almost half of India’s overall rooftop solar capacity. Of this, ~88% is in just ten states.
Gujarat and Maharashtra lead in total rooftop solar installations. But, when it comes to the residential segment, the leaderboard changes. Assam and Odisha are among the top ten states for residential rooftop installations but are not in the top ten list when C&I installations are also included. Similarly, while Tamil Nadu and Karnataka are prominent states when it comes to total rooftop solar installations, they are outside the top ten in residential installations, suggesting C&I installations weigh heavily in these states. Notably, in Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Kerala, rooftop solar capacity additions have picked up in recent years, and more than 50% of total rooftop capacity is coming from residential installations.
The consumer category mix matters because residential and C&I consumers have different electricity consumption patterns relative to solar generation. C&I consumers typically have greater overlap between electricity consumption and solar generation, and their rooftop systems are strategically sized to maximise on-site consumption. This reduces surplus generation exported to the grid and, consequently, the temporal mismatch between solar generation and electricity consumption. Household electricity demand, by contrast, is typically lower during solar hours and higher during non-solar hours, particularly in the evening. As a result, the grid effectively acts as a “nearly free virtual battery” for residential prosumers, absorbing surplus daytime generation and supplying electricity when household demand rises.
As residential rooftop solar scales, therefore, states with a higher share of residential prosumers such as Kerala, Gujarat and Maharashtra could see greater volumes of daytime exports followed by evening imports, increasing the importance of grid flexibility.
As rooftop solar penetration rises in states, both the scale and prosumer mix will matter for the grid. States where rooftop solar accounts for a larger share of peak demand are already encountering grid integration challenges. At the same time, the consumer categories driving rooftop growth will shape how it interacts with the grid, including how much generation is consumed on-site and how much is exported.
The rapid expansion of residential rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, alongside existing net metering arrangements, makes this interaction increasingly important to examine. The question for states is therefore shifting from simply how much rooftop solar is being added to how that growing capacity is affecting the grid.
Rooftop solar is beginning to change the demand pattern the grid sees, as well as its magnitude. During solar hours, consumers meet part of their electricity demand behind the meter, reducing the net load seen by distribution companies (DISCOMs) even though their underlying consumption remains unchanged.
