health-tech-5502654527.fulltext:
Malathy Iyer is Senior Editor (Health) at The Times of India, Mum... Read More
Malathy Iyer is Senior Editor (Health) at The Times of India, Mumbai. She writes mainly on health-related subjects.Read Less
Mumbai: A quiet shift is underway in cancer care in India. Over the past six months, more patients have been prescribed immunotherapy, one of the newer advances in cancer treatment that has remained beyond the reach of many because of its prohibitive cost.
Dr Imran Shaikh of Kokilaben Dhirubhai Ambani Hospital in Andheri says his prescriptions for nivolumab have risen by more than 50% in the past six months following the arrival of a cheaper biosimilar.
“My patients are responding well to the drug. People who were earlier unsure whether they could afford a cycle costing over a lakh of rupees are comfortable with the new price tag of Rs 30,000,” Dr Shaikh told TOI.
While it is too early to quantify the overall increase in prescriptions, the access gap has been stark. In 2022, only 2.8% of patients eligible for immunotherapy were receiving it, according to a TMC study. Dr Jyoti Bajpai, director of precision oncology at Apollo Hospitals in Navi Mumbai, who co-authored the study while at TMC, says there has been a “substantial increase” in prescriptions.
Dr Kumar Prabhash, head of medical oncology at Tata Memorial Hospital in Parel, points to the gains immunotherapy has brought in some cancers, particularly melanoma, or skin cancer.
“Earlier barely five out of 100 patients had long-term survival, but survival has now increased to 50% with immunotherapy,” said Dr Kumar, adding that some patients diagnosed with advanced lung cancer are now living for five years or longer.
A price cut is not enough
Despite the progress, India lags behind some countries in the availability of checkpoint inhibitors. Dr Shaikh said India offers only seven such drugs, compared with 35 in China. Apart from nivolumab, he said, the other six available in India are imported and can cost lakhs of rupees for a course of treatment.
But the cost of cancer treatment could come down further following National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s move, effective Nov 8, to cap trade margins on 137 anti-cancer medicines. The measure is projected to generate annual savings of Rs 2,500 crore and could offer relief across a range of treatments.
But lower prices may not automatically translate into savings for patients. K M Gopakumar of Third World Network cautioned that hospitals that require patients to purchase medicines through their own pharmacies may have little incentive to stock cheaper alternatives.
“Hospitals may favour more expensive original medicines because of higher margins. The cheaper versions may thus not be available to the patients as a result,” he said.
Four more versions of nivolumab are expected to enter the market soon, potentially driving prices down further. “The price of the drug may drop from Rs 30,000 now to Rs 10,000, but will any place stock medicines that offer them lower margin?” he said.
Dr Kumar said it remained to be seen whether the benefits of lower prices would reach patients. “We at Tata Memorial Centre make arrangements in such a way that patients have to pay the least for medicines,” he said.
For Dr Bajpai, the real test is whether advances in medical and precision oncology reach patients regardless of their ability to pay. Cheaper biosimilars and evidence-based dosing strategies offer a way forward, but their promise will be realised only if lower costs translate into meaningful access to treatment.
“The real success of innovation is not just how long patients live, but how many patients can access the treatment they need — without financial hardship,” said Dr Bajpai.
Immunotherapy, however, is not a magic bullet. Its effectiveness varies according to the cancer type, stage and individual patient.
“No medicine will work on all patients. Every medicine has indications in which it works and others in which it does not. Ditto with checkpoint inhibitors and other immunotherapy drugs,” said Dr Kumar.
“Our research into short-course and low-dose approaches reflects the difficult choices patients face when cost becomes a barrier. agritech-8ce16b82df.fulltext:
India has completed the creation of 11 crore Farmer IDs five months ahead of the March 31, 2027 deadline, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan announced on October 24. He described the milestone as an important step towards strengthening digital agriculture and enhancing access to government benefits.
The target was achieved by the night of October 23 under the Centre’s Digital Agriculture Mission, which is implemented by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare. The Farmer ID system provides farmers with unique digital identities, enabling faster and more transparent access to government schemes, bank loans, crop insurance and disaster relief.
Chouhan congratulated farmers nationwide and attributed the success to coordinated efforts between the Central and state governments, Union Territory administrations and field-level officials.
The Farmer ID system aims to reduce paperwork and eliminate the need for farmers to submit documents or undergo repeated verification to access various government schemes. The Ministry anticipates that this system will simplify access to agricultural credit products such as loans and Kisan Credit Cards, while improving transparency in compensation under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana and disaster relief programmes.
Additionally, the digital framework is expected to strengthen transparency in procurement at the Minimum Support Price, reduce intermediary roles and enable direct payments to farmers’ bank accounts.
The Digital Agriculture Mission received Union Cabinet approval on September 2, 2024. It involves developing Digital Public Infrastructure to establish a verified database of farmers and enhance the delivery of agricultural services. More than six crore farmers have already benefited directly through the Farmer ID-based service delivery system, according to the Ministry.
The verified database is intended to eliminate duplication and fraudulent claims, improve coordination among government departments and strengthen monitoring and implementation of welfare schemes.
Chouhan emphasised the achievement as a reflection of cooperative federalism, recognising the contributions of officials at central, state, district and village levels. States and Union Territories are also working, in accordance with applicable regulations, to include tenant farmers and actual cultivators in the digital platform to ensure no eligible beneficiaries are excluded.
The Ministry aims to reinforce the Farmer Registry following the principle of ‘Minimum Government, Maximum Governance’. Chouhan underlined that the initiative would foster transparent and farmer-centric governance, urging farmers to adopt modern technologies and avail themselves of government scheme benefits.
The government views the Farmer ID system as a crucial element of a modern agricultural ecosystem, intended to streamline service delivery and support the vision of a developed India with prosperous farmers.

indian-startups-386c83896b.headline: Garuda Aerospace’s FY26 revenue jumps 67% to Rs 206 Cr; profit rise 42%
indian-startups-386c83896b.fulltext:
Drone technology startup Garuda Aerospace reported a strong 67% year-on-year revenue growth in FY26 while maintaining profitability, with net profit at Rs 26 crore as the Chennai-based company is preparing to go public soon as it recently received SEBI nod for Rs 1,000 crore IPO.
Garuda’s revenue from operations rose to Rs 206 crore in the fiscal year ended March 2026,compared to Rs 123.5 crore in FY25, according to its financial statements filed with the Registrar of Companies (RoC).
Garuda Aerospace designs and manufactures drones for applications across agriculture, defence, infrastructure, mining and disaster management. Besides drone manufacturing, the firm also offers Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) and operates a DGCA-approved remote pilot training programme. 
Revenue from sale of services surged 84.1% to Rs 106.46 crore in FY26 from Rs 57.83 crore in FY25, while revenue from sale of products grew 66.2% to Rs 99.50 crore from Rs 59.85 crore during the same period.
On the expense front, the cost of materials, remains the largest expense component, rose 62% to Rs 117 crore in FY26 from Rs 72.21 crore in FY25. Meanwhile, employee benefit expenses declined 16.2% to Rs 8 crore from Rs 9.55 crore.
Legal and professional charges surged 94.6% to Rs 12.88 crore from Rs 6.62 crore. Other overheads such as impairment loss on financial assets, depreciation & amortization expenses, travelling added another Rs 34.12 crore to the total cost.
Overall, Garuda’s total expenses grew 73.7% to Rs 172 crore in the last fiscal year compared to Rs 99 crore in FY25.
Despite the increase in costs, the company reported a 41.5% increase in net profit to Rs 26 crore in FY26 from Rs 18.37 crore in FY25. Its return on capital employed (ROCE) stood and EBITDA margin stood  at 14.71% and 18.97% respectively.
On a unit level, Garuda spent Rs 0.83 to generate every rupee of operating revenue in FY26, compared to Rs 0.80 in FY25. 
At the end of March 2026, the firm’s total current assets increased to Rs 303 crore from Rs 176 crore, while its cash and bank balance stood at Rs 5.2 crore.
Garuda Aerospace pre-filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with SEBI through the confidential route in April. The proposed Rs 1,000 crore IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 750 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of Rs 250 crore by existing shareholders.

global-economics-f9daf661cc.headline: Ukraine seeks Starlink alternative after Musk's satellite disruptions: What Nokia and ICEYE are building?
global-economics-f9daf661cc.fulltext:
Swati GandhiUpdated24 Oct 2026, 10:31 AM IST Days after Ukraine reported restrictions on its access to Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services provided by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect, Kyiv is now partnering with the Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE to develop new defence and satellite communications capabilities. In a press release on Thursday (local time), Nokia announced that the two companies had signed a Letter of Intent (LoI) with Ukraine's defence ministry to explore cooperation in space. The partnership aims to support Kyiv's defence capabilities, particularly by building sovereign satellite communications. According to reports, the goal is to develop a secure satellite communications system of Kyiv’s own. Earlier this month, the two Finnish companies also announced a collaboration to create secure, sovereign and high-performance broadband satellite communications systems in low Earth orbit (LEO) for governments, Nokia said. These systems would support missions ranging from defence and border security to emergency services and disaster response. The satellite communications systems will give nations ownership and control of the satellites, ground segment and terminals. According to Space.com, ICEYE is already aiding Kyiv's defence effort. ICEYE and its US subsidiary jointly run a network of Earth-observation satellites in low Earth orbit, using synthetic aperture radar to monitor the planet. Ukraine draws on imagery from the constellation to support intelligence gathering and operational planning. The partnership was announced during the Finnish prime minister's visit to Ukraine. Commenting on the collaboration, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security. We must all rely on capabilities that we can control. The Letter of Intent between the Ministry of Defense, ICEYE, and Nokia is an important step in this direction. I thank Finland and the Prime Minister of Finland for their consistent support. We value partners who not only help Ukraine, but also work with us to build Europe’s long-term security." Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE, said, "Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls. We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain it to continuing that support today." Separately, Zelenskyy has also announced a partnership with Norway to jointly develop air defence and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield. The push for satellite communications under Ukrainian control comes amid growing concerns over Kyiv’s reliance on SpaceX, after recent service restrictions disrupted connections on fast-moving drones. The development comes at a time when Kyiv has been struggling to intercept and launch drones after Musk's SpaceX reportedly restricted the country's access to Starshield, the military version of the system. According to Zelenskyy, connection speeds on Starlink, a service Ukraine used for some military activities, including defence against Russian missile attacks, had been reduced. Both US President Donald Trump and Musk have denied responsibility for the unannounced restrictions, which Kyiv first reported on 14 October and said remained in place as of Friday (local time). Trump told reporters on Friday that he would call the billionaire to have the restrictions lifted. Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this week that four of Europe's major telecom groups, Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone, are also considering satellite mobile services of their own to lessen reliance on providers outside the European Union and compete with Musk’s Starlink. ai-ce859b8f57.headline: Flipkart’s super.money spent Rs 341 crore on marketing to earn Rs 292 crore in revenue in FY26
ai-ce859b8f57.fulltext:
Flipkart-backed Unified Payments Interface (UPI) app super.money more than tripled its operating revenue to Rs 292.4 crore in FY26 from Rs 88.8 crore a year earlier, on the back of strong growth in its loan marketplace business.
However, its net loss widened 78% to Rs 263.8 crore from Rs 147.8 crore, filings with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) showed.
Launched as a payments app in 2024 after Flipkart separated from PhonePe, super.money has since become one of India’s top 5 UPI apps by transaction volume. The app processed over 400 million transactions per month for five consecutive months through September, per data from the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), which manages the UPI system.
Last year, super.money acquired Y Combinator-backed fintech startup BharatX for an undisclosed amount, according to the Economic Times. The acquisition helped the company expand its credit offerings, particularly checkout financing products such as buy now, pay later (BNPL) and consumer durable loans. It also enabled super.money to extend credit on UPI on Flipkart and direct-to-consumer (D2C) platforms.
Reports have suggested that super.money is also mulling a stock broking foray. However, an official confirmation is not available in the public domain.
super.money’s core business spans UPI payments and loan marketplace services. It facilitates digital payments and loans through partnerships with banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), earning revenue from these arrangements.
Loan marketplace services contributed Rs 247.8 crore, accounting for roughly 85% of the company’s total revenue in FY26.
Other operating revenue stood at Rs 44.6 crore. In its annual financial statements, the company did not mention what counts as other operating revenue or how much it earned from this vertical in FY25.
Consumer-facing UPI apps tend to spend heavily on marketing to acquire customers in their early years of operations. Monetisation levers kick in later via credit and commerce. And this is exactly how it is playing out at super.money.
The Flipkart-backed fintech saw its total expenses climb 130% to Rs 557.1 crore from Rs 241.8 crore a year earlier.
Business promotion expenses: super.money spent Rs 341 crore on marketing in FY26, a more than threefold increase from Rs 101.3 crore last year.
Employee benefit expense: Stood at Rs 138.1 crore, including Rs 36.8 crore in ESOP costs.
Marketplace charges: The company managed to cut its spending under this head to Rs 15.6 crore, compared with Rs 43.5 crore a year earlier.
In March this year, super.money, along with Flipkart’s other Singapore-based subsidiaries including logistics arm eKart, fashion e-commerce platform Myntra and travel platform Cleartrip, among others, merged into Flipkart Internet, as part of the company’s restructuring ahead of a potential initial public offering (IPO).
Overall, Flipkart Group posted a consolidated net loss of Rs 8,468 crore against operating revenue of Rs 1.45 lakh crore in FY26.

global-economics-86b85b401a.headline: German drone maker Quantum Systems claims 483-mph speed for battery-powered experimental aircraft

LivemintPublished24 Oct 2026, 08:23 PM IST
German drone manufacturer Quantum Systems has announced that its battery-powered experimental aircraft, Apex Recordhunter, reached a speed of 483 mph (777 km/h) during a record attempt, potentially setting a new benchmark for battery-electric flight.
However, the achievement has not yet been officially confirmed, as the aircraft must complete a return flight to account for the effects of wind, reported Interesting Engineering.
The latest test highlights advances in electric propulsion technology and provides engineers with an opportunity to assess the performance and limitations of battery-powered aircraft operating at extremely high speeds.
Quantum Systems said the findings from the experiment would contribute to its ongoing drone development programmes, including technologies designed to counter fast-moving aerial threats.
The latest reported speed exceeds the 434 mph (699 km/h) achieved by the Apex Recordhunter during a test in June. At the time, the company described the performance as an unofficial world-best for a battery-electric flying object.
Developed by Quantum Systems' experimental N3XT team in Germany over approximately a year, the Apex Recordhunter is a technology demonstrator rather than an operational aircraft.
The project allows engineers to evaluate electric propulsion, energy management and high-speed flight performance. The latest run pushed the aircraft's reported speed to more than 200 metres per second, demonstrating the power requirements associated with rapid battery-electric flight.
Despite the reported achievement, the company has not disclosed detailed specifications for the aircraft's battery capacity, motor, energy consumption or flight duration.
Quantum Systems said the aircraft uses specialised battery cells developed by a Porsche subsidiary. However, detailed technical information about the battery pack and propulsion system has not been released.
Achieving high speeds with battery-powered aircraft requires careful management of energy consumption and propulsion performance.
The aircraft must generate sufficient power to maintain its speed while preserving stability and operating within the limitations of its electrical systems.
The Apex project is intended to help engineers understand these challenges and identify improvements that could be applied to future aircraft designs.
The reported 483-mph run is not yet an officially established record. A return leg is required to account for wind effects and validate the aircraft's performance under the applicable record-attempt procedure.
Quantum Systems said the experience gained through the project would inform its future development efforts.
Beyond experimental flight, Quantum Systems said technologies developed through the Apex programme could support its work on interceptor drones designed to counter increasingly fast aerial threats.
The company has pointed to Russia's jet-powered Geran drones, which can reportedly reach speeds of 311 to 373 mph (500 to 600 km/h).
The increasing speed of such aircraft creates challenges for interception systems, potentially requiring faster and more capable drones to respond effectively.
Quantum Systems said its work on electric propulsion, energy management and high-speed flight was helping inform the development of interceptor technologies.
However, the company has clarified that the Apex Recordhunter itself is not a weapon and does not share hardware with its combat systems.
The Apex Recordhunter programme illustrates how experimental aircraft can help manufacturers evaluate emerging propulsion technologies before applying the findings to other systems.
Although the reported speed remains subject to official confirmation, the test provides additional data on the potential capabilities of battery-electric aircraft.
Quantum Systems has not yet announced when the record attempt will be formally validated. The results of further testing will help determine how the technology could contribute to future high-speed drone development.

Apoorva AjithPublished23 Oct 2026, 10:46 PM IST The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has imposed penalties totalling ₹11.5 crore on Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy Pvt. Ltd (ASTAPL) and its directors, and barred them from accessing the securities markets for periods of up to two years for providing unregistered investment advisory and research analyst activities. In a final order issued on Friday, the market regulator directed ASTAPL and its founder Avadhut Dinkar Sathe to disgorge and refund ₹546.17 crore to eligible investors and participants who paid for its unregistered services. It has also ordered a deposit of ₹67.87 crore in interest with Sebi’s Investor Protection and Education Fund. Sebi imposed a penalty of ₹6 crore on ASTAPL, ₹4 crore on Sathe and ₹1.5 crore on Gouri Avadhut Sathe, another director. Sebi also prohibited ASTAPL and Avadhut Sathe from accessing or dealing in the securities markets, directly or indirectly, for two years or until they comply with the refund direction, whichever is later. Gouri Sathe has been barred for six months. Sebi had issued an interim order on the matter on 5 December 2025. The regulator’s action follows its findings that the academy’s activities went beyond financial education and included investment advice and research-related services without the required registrations. The order cites recommendations on specific securities, including buy and sell calls, price targets and stop-loss levels, delivered through live sessions and WhatsApp communications. The order directs ASTAPL and Sathe to publish refund notices within 30 days of receiving it in two national newspapers—one English and one Hindi—and a local-language newspaper. The notices must explain how eligible claimants can seek refunds. Payments must be made through electronic banking channels, with an audit trail, and the process must be independently certified by a peer-reviewed chartered accountant. Sebi has also restricted the sale of assets by ASTAPL and Sathe, except where necessary to execute refunds, and ordered debit restrictions on their bank accounts until the required transfers are made. Sebi also objected to promotional material and testimonials that highlighted unusually high trading profits. Its examination of trading data found losses, including net trading losses, and the regulator said misleading promotional claims continued even after it issued a warning in March 2024. Gouri Sathe’s liability was treated separately: Sebi said that it had not found she personally provided the services, devised the arrangement or obtained wrongful gains. Mid-career professionals drive healthcare GCC hiring in 2026: Report

India creates 11 crore Farmer IDs five months ahead of March 2027 deadline
India has achieved its target of creating 11 crore Farmer IDs five months before the March 31, 2027, deadline, Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said. The digital identity system aims to streamline access to government schemes and agricultural services.
                                        
                    Published Date - 24 October 2026, 03:49 PM 
                                    
                                                
                
                            
New Delhi: Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare and Rural Development, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, on Saturday, said India has achieved its target of creating 11 crore Farmer IDs five months ahead of the March 31, 2027, deadline.
The milestone achieved under the Digital Agriculture Mission will help benefit various schemes to be provided in a transparent manner, Chouhan said in an X post.
                                            
                
Further, a statement from the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare said the Farmer ID acts as a unique digital identity to give farmers transparent, efficient and timely access to government schemes, bank credit, crop insurance and disaster relief while reducing paperwork and repeated verification.
Over 6 crore farmers across the country have so far received direct benefits under various schemes through the Farmer ID-based service delivery system. A verified farmer database was linked with agricultural services, which eliminated fraud and the need for duplicate verification.
The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, state governments and field-level officials worked in coordination to achieve it five months ahead of schedule, the minister said.
Chouhan said the Farmer ID system would significantly reduce the need for farmers to repeatedly visit government offices and banks or submit the same documents for different schemes. Farmers often had to provide documents repeatedly to access various benefits, resulting in a loss of both time and money.
States and Union Territories are also taking specific steps, in accordance with applicable rules, to bring tenant farmers and actual cultivators onto the digital platform
The initiative will strengthen delivery of services such as Kisan Credit Cards, Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana claims and Minimum Support Price procurement, the statement said.
The digital system will help eliminate the role of intermediaries in the procurement process and ensure that farmers receive the full value due for their produce.

agritech-dd3127892d.headline: India Creates 11 Crore Farmer IDs Ahead of March 2027 Deadline
agritech-dd3127892d.fulltext:
India has reached a major milestone in its digital agriculture programme, with the government announcing the creation of 11 crore Farmer IDs five months ahead of the scheduled deadline.
According to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, the target was completed by the night of 23 October 2026. The original deadline, set for 31 March 2027, was established as part of the government’s effort to build a more integrated digital system for agricultural services.
Editorial Insight
Key Highlights
Important points readers should notice.
Issue/Event: India achieved the target of creating 11 crore Farmer IDs under its Digital Agriculture Mission.
Location: Nationwide, through coordination between the Union government, state governments, Union Territories and field-level administrations.
Authority/Organisation: The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, with Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan announcing the milestone.
Action Taken: The government completed the target by the night of 23 October 2026, ahead of the original deadline of 31 March 2027.
Impact: The system is intended to simplify verification and improve access to agricultural schemes, credit, insurance and disaster relief, but actual benefits depend on eligibility, accurate records and implementation.
The achievement comes under the Digital Agriculture Mission, which aims to develop digital infrastructure for agriculture and create a more reliable system for identifying farmers and connecting them with relevant public services.
What is a Farmer ID?
A Farmer ID is a unique digital identity designed to help identify farmers within the agricultural services system. It is part of the wider AgriStack framework, which seeks to connect verified farmer records with relevant agricultural services.
Editorial Analysis
Why This Matters
Less repetitive paperwork: A consistent digital identity may reduce the need for farmers to submit the same information repeatedly. Access to financial services: Verified records may help simplify parts of the process for bank loans and Kisan Credit Cards, subject to lender requirements. Agricultural risk protection: Better-connected records could support the administration of crop insurance and disaster relief. Public accountability: Digital systems can make it easier to monitor service delivery, identify duplicate records and review administrative processes. Inclusion of cultivators: Tenant farmers and actual cultivators need clear, accessible procedures so that digital registration does not unfairly exclude eligible people. Data protection: As more agricultural services become digitally connected, appropriate safeguards, transparent use of information and effective correction mechanisms remain important.
The government says the system can reduce repeated paperwork and the need to submit the same information multiple times when accessing different schemes. A more consistent record may also help government departments coordinate their services and verify eligibility more efficiently.
The system is intended to make the delivery of agricultural support more transparent. Its effectiveness, however, depends on the accuracy of records, the inclusion of eligible farmers and how well different services use the digital infrastructure.
How could the ID help farmers?
The Agriculture Ministry has identified several areas where Farmer IDs are expected to simplify access to services.
Bank loans and Kisan Credit Cards: A verified digital identity may reduce repeated document checks during loan-related processes. The actual requirements will continue to depend on the relevant bank and lending rules.
Crop insurance: The government says the system is intended to support more transparent assessment and payment processes under crop insurance programmes, including the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana.
Disaster relief: A verified database may help authorities identify eligible farmers and coordinate relief during emergencies.
Minimum Support Price procurement: The digital system is intended to improve verification during procurement and reduce the scope for intermediaries to interfere with the process.
These are the intended benefits described by the government. The announcement does not establish that every farmer will immediately receive all these services through the ID alone.
More than six crore farmers reported to have received benefits
The Ministry said that more than six crore farmers had already received direct benefits under various schemes through Farmer ID-based service delivery.
It also said that linking verified farmer records with agricultural services was helping improve coordination between government departments and monitoring of scheme implementation.
The announcement does not provide a complete breakdown of the schemes, benefit amounts or reporting period associated with the six-crore figure. Therefore, it should not be interpreted as the number of farmers who received a new payment on 24 October.
Bringing tenant farmers and actual cultivators into the system
The Ministry has also highlighted efforts by states and Union Territories to bring tenant farmers and actual cultivators onto the digital platform, subject to applicable rules.
This is an important implementation issue because agricultural land ownership and the person actually cultivating a field are not always the same. State-level rules and verification procedures can influence how such farmers are recorded.
For the system to deliver its intended benefits fairly, eligible cultivators must be able to understand the applicable requirements and correct errors in their records. The latest announcement does not provide a single nationwide procedure covering every tenant or sharecropper situation.
What the milestone does—and does not—mean
The creation of 11 crore Farmer IDs represents progress towards the government’s digital agriculture target. It does not, on its own, prove that all eligible farmers are registered, that every record is error-free or that every connected scheme is operating without delays.
The next measure of success will be how effectively the system serves farmers in practice. That includes accurate records, accessible correction procedures, protection of personal information and reliable access to the services linked to the platform.

other-interests-0373036c88.headline: Astronomers unlock a mystery hidden in van Gogh’s The Starry Night
other-interests-0373036c88.fulltext:
Researchers say they’ve identified the constellation depicted in Vincent van Gogh’s famous painting The Starry Night—and that the discovery changes what historians have assumed about the timing of the artwork’s creation.
The painting, now in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City, is said to date back to mid-June 1889, when van Gogh was in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in France. But astronomers seeking to use the painting’s stars to pin down the exact time and place it was created have reached conflicting conclusions.
In a paper published on October 22 in Scientific Reports, researchers identified the stars in The Starry Night as those of the V-shaped Hyades cluster within the Taurus constellation, as observed on July 22, 1889.
On supporting science journalism

“To my eyes, the star cluster in The Starry Night was the Hyades in Taurus. But earlier studies explained it as Aries,” says space researcher Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, who is first author of the paper. “At that moment, I was sure this painting was worth studying.”
To find the constellation in The Starry Night, the researchers used a software program called Procrustes, which looked for patterns based on the shape formed by the relative positions of a group of stars rather than likely artistic embellishments such as size or color. This “shape analysis” technique matched five stars in the painting with five stars in the Hyades cluster, which had the strongest statistical fit out of any of the alternative constellations tested, including Aries, which had previously been proposed to be the constellation in the center of the painting. The researchers also tested this method on a van Gogh painting with a known constellation in it, the Big Dipper in Starry Night over the Rhône, and found its match had a comparably strong result to that of The Starry Night and Hyades.
To bolster their case, Kim and his colleagues looked to evidence from van Gogh’s letters at the time he was working on The Starry Night to show that perhaps he had painted it in several sessions, with the stars being observed from late July. Although van Gogh mentioned “a new study” of the starry sky in a June 18, 1889, letter, the researchers say that doesn’t mean he had finished the painting. Van Gogh’s letters also make no mention of Aries, despite his regular references to observing Venus, which was close to that constellation in the sky. “The stars of Aries are relatively faint, hardly enough to inspire a painter” at dawn, Kim says, which was when van Gogh often watched the stars.
Another argument against a mid-June date for The Starry Night is the lunar cycle—at that time, the moon would have been in a waning gibbous phase, with its sunlit side appearing as a lopsided oval. Yet the painting shows a waning crescent moon, as it would have been in a late-July sky. Kim also visited Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in June and July 2019 to fully capture van Gogh’s field of view from the precise location where he painted The Starry Night. Kim’s observations there, he says, further confirm the match with the Hyades cluster.
“During this time, van Gogh’s view of the sky was quite restricted” from his window at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole mental asylum, says James Beattie, a Hubble fellow at NASA. “If the identification holds, we can look up today and recognize the same stars van Gogh saw.”
Despite the study’s thoroughness, of course, for a painting as iconic as The Starry Night, there will always be competing versions of an origin story.
“The calculated position of brilliant Venus, in relation to the V shape of the Hyades asterism, does not match the painting,” says Don Olson, a self-proclaimed “celestial sleuth” for astronomical artwork and a professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at Texas State University. The researchers’ conclusions “require strong evidence to overcome Vincent van Gogh’s plain statement that ‘at last I have... a new study of a starry sky’ ... on June 18, 1889.”
Although there are still mysteries to resolve, Kim says the burden of proof has now reversed to proving the painting could not have been made in late July.
“The Starry Night spoke to an astronomer like me,” Kim says. “I listened to its voice.”

other-interests-590a246ab6.headline: Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' depicts the sky on July 22, 1889, researchers find
other-interests-590a246ab6.fulltext:
Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' depicts the sky on July 22, 1889, researchers find
This could be the actual Starry Night.
Researchers think they might have pinpointed the exact night sky that we see depicted in Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "The Starry Night."
Perhaps one of the most famous paintings in modern history, Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" carries a legacy that continues to inspire and mystify generation after generation. But while you might see in its swirls of color and bright spots of starlight a night sky derived purely from imagination, some scientists think it represents an actual view — one that includes a waning crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades cluster. And they may know exactly when this sky appeared..
In a new study, researchers suggest that "The Starry Night" depicts the pre-dawn sky seen around July 22, 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where Van Gogh painted it. But while this sky happens to perfectly match the one depicted in the artwork, art historians have long thought that Van Gogh painted this piece in June. Could these findings shift the date of this legendary artwork?
Finding a painted sky
This investigation started decades ago with art historian Albert Boime and astronomer George Abell at UCLA in 1984 and continued in the following years with astronomer Charles Whitney at Harvard University. However, these earlier analyses did not agree with one another, and there was no true consensus about exactly when the sky matched with the painting.
So the question remained, lingering in the minds of those with a shared love for both art and space. And a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of South Korean robotic telescope company SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, picked up the search once more.
"When they see a fragment of a starry sky, observational astronomers like me and amateur astronomers alike will want to solve the puzzle. I am simply someone who pursued that process a little more actively," Kim told Space.com.
But how did Kim's team come to their conclusion, after others had failed to nail down a date over the decades? In short, "we analyzed the painting astronomically, analyzed documents about his situation in July 1889, and then carried out ecological and meteorological investigations," Kim said.
To start with, the team analyzed the sky from the exact location in Saint-Rémy where Van Gogh is said to have painted "The Starry Night." They then used observational geometry to map the historical night sky.
"Modern telescopes are equipped with a function called astrometry, which compares an image of the night sky with celestial coordinates stored in a computer and automatically extracts the coordinates of the image," Kim said. "We used Procrustes analysis, a method that compares only the 'shape' of two sets of points. After matching their position, size and rotation, it measures how similar the two shapes are from the differences that remain (the residuals)."
"Because a star cluster on the canvas may be larger or smaller than in reality and slightly tilted, this method was the right fit. It allowed us to explain, in quantitative terms, what earlier studies had described only qualitatively as 'resembling a certain constellation,'" Kim added.
But this quantitative analysis wasn't enough to say for sure that this was the right-fitting sky, as different constellations could fit to a similar degree, Kim explained. To get closer to their answer, the team combined their analysis with a deep dive through history.
"We also checked whether the stars were actually in that part of the pre-dawn sky on that date, whether they fall within the painter’s field of view, and whether the appearance of the moon and Venus matches the painting. It was the Hyades that satisfied all of these conditions," Kim said.
Exploring astro-art history
As mentioned, the date of this matching sky comes in late July, a month after art historians think Van Gogh painted "The Starry Night." But the researchers suggest that their findings could provide evidence to support the idea that the work was actually painted in July.
Letters written by Van Gogh as early as 1888 describe his desire to paint a star-filled sky. A letter dated April 12, 1888 reads: "A starry sky, for example, well — it’s a thing that I’d like to try to do, just as in the daytime I’ll try to paint a green meadow studded with dandelions."
Kim followed these letters through the months to try and find more information that could potentially alleviate the discrepancy between the matching skies and the actual month the painting was created. Kim pointed to a letter from between late May and early June 1889 that reads: "This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big."
Kim drew on "personal imagination" to find ties between Van Gogh's sky observations in these months and what they might mean for the painting's timeline, Kim shared, so this doesn't definitively change the view of this painting's history. However, Kim suggested that these records could indicate that Van Gogh was repeatedly looking up and watching the pre-dawn sky, which could have led to him seeing this exact sky on July 22.
The painting itself even ignites uncertainty among art historians. As the researchers cite in their new paper, leading art historians see "The Starry Night" as stylistically different from Van Gogh's other works during the month of June, drawing further questions over the date painted.
"What our study shows is that the sky in the painting matches, in both observation and shape, the real pre-dawn sky around July 22. So, what we propose is the possibility that Vincent conceived the idea in June and completed the painting after July 22," Kim said.
However, "I think further research in art history and conservation science could shed more light on this question," Kim added.
This work was described in a study published Oct. 22 in the journal Scientific Reports.
